title: Beyond Pangong: 7 Offbeat Ladakh Destinations Worth the Detour
excerpt: From a Balti village on the Line of Control to a cliffside monastery in Zanskar, Ladakh's quieter corners reward travellers who venture past the standard tourist loop.
body:
Key Takeaways
  • Ladakh saw a 43% increase in tourist arrivals from January to May 2026.
  • Seven offbeat destinations offer unique cultural and adventure experiences away from crowded tourist spots.
  • Inner Line Permits are required for certain border-adjacent areas, limiting access.
  • Homestays provide affordable and community-driven accommodation across these lesser-known locations.

  • Ladakh recorded a 43% surge in tourist arrivals between January and May 2026, but most visitors still cluster around Pangong Lake and Nubra Valley — leaving dozens of destinations virtually empty.
  • Seven lesser-known spots — Turtuk, Hanle, Tso Moriri, Uleytokpo, Sumda Chun, Dha-Hanu, and Phugtal — offer distinct cultural, wildlife, and adventure experiences that the standard Leh circuit misses.
  • Inner Line Permits are required for border-adjacent areas including Turtuk, Hanle, and Dha-Hanu; the June-to-September window is the only reliable travel season for most of these destinations.
  • Homestays are the primary accommodation across all seven locations, making offbeat Ladakh travel both affordable and community-driven.

Ladakh is having a record year. Between January and May 2026, the Union Territory welcomed 117,546 tourists — a 43% jump over the same period last year, according to official data cited by Lieutenant Governor V.K. Saxena. May alone saw a 121% spike. But dig into the numbers and a familiar pattern emerges: the bulk of visitors still funnel into Pangong Lake and Nubra Valley, leaving vast stretches of the region largely untouched.

That imbalance is precisely what makes Ladakh's offbeat destinations so compelling right now. Beyond the well-worn loop lie villages, lakes, and monasteries that offer something the crowded shoreline of Pangong no longer can — solitude, cultural depth, and the kind of travel that feels earned rather than packaged.

Turtuk: India's Last Village Before the Pakistan Border

Roughly 205 km from Leh, tucked into the Shyok Valley, Turtuk is one of the few Balti-populated villages on the Indian side of the Line of Control. Until the 1971 Indo-Pak war, it was part of Pakistan-administered Baltistan. The Indian Army captured it during the conflict, and it remained closed to outsiders until 2010.

What draws travellers today is the village's distinct cultural identity. The roughly 4,000 residents speak Balti — an ancient dialect with Persian roots — and practise Islam, a striking contrast to Buddhist-majority Ladakh. Visitors can explore the Royal Palace Museum, run by a descendant of the Yabgo dynasty, walk through apricot orchards that blanket the village in green every summer, and photograph centuries-old stone-and-wood houses with carved balconies. The apricots, sun-dried or pressed into oil, are practically Turtuk's calling card.

Hanle: Stargazing Under the Darkest Skies in India

Perched at roughly 4,500 metres on the Changthang Plateau, Hanle is home to the Indian Astronomical Observatory, operated by the Indian Institute of Astrophysics — one of the world's highest optical telescope sites. In December 2022, the area was designated India's first Dark Sky Reserve, covering more than 1,000 square kilometres of high-altitude desert where outdoor lighting is restricted to protect Bortle-1 skies, the darkest classification that exists.

Visitor numbers climbed to an estimated 10,000 in 2024, according to travel industry data, up from just a few thousand before the pandemic. Local villagers trained as astro-guides run homestays and telescope sessions, meaning tourism revenue flows directly into the community.

Tso Moriri: Pangong's Quieter, Wilder Cousin

Sitting at 4,522 metres, Tso Moriri is one of India's highest lakes and, unlike Pangong, lies entirely within Indian territory. The lake is a Ramsar-recognised wetland sheltering migratory birds including the black-necked crane and bar-headed goose, plus Himalayan marmots and, occasionally, the elusive snow leopard in surrounding hills.

On its shores sits Korzok, one of the world's highest permanently inhabited villages, home to a 300-year-old monastery and the Changpa — semi-nomadic herders who raise pashmina goats producing the world's finest cashmere wool. A night here, sipping butter tea in a Changpa tent while the lake shifts from turquoise to navy at sunset, is among the most authentic experiences left in Ladakh.

Four More Worth the Drive

Exploring Offbeat Ladakh
›Turtuk: Balti culture and apricot orchards.
›Hanle: India's first Dark Sky Reserve.
›Tso Moriri: Home to migratory birds and pashmina goats.
›Dha-Hanu: Unique Indo-Aryan community.
›Phugtal Monastery: Cliffside Buddhist retreat.

Uleytokpo, just 70 km from Leh on the Leh-Kargil highway, is a riverside settlement along the Indus popular with birdwatchers. It doubles as a base for visiting Alchi and Likir monasteries without the bustle of Leh town.

Sumda Chun Monastery, accessible only via a full-day trek through a narrow gorge, houses 11th-century murals linked to the translator Rinchen Zangpo. The absence of any motorable road keeps visitor numbers naturally low and the atmosphere contemplative.

Dha and Hanu, twin villages near Kargil, are home to the Brokpa community — a small Indo-Aryan ethnic group whose elaborate floral headgear, oral traditions, and customs set them apart from the rest of Ladakh. Visits require an Inner Line Permit and are usually arranged through registered operators.

Phugtal Monastery in Zanskar clings to a cliff above the Tsarap Chu river, earning its nickname as Ladakh's "honeycomb." Built around a cave used by Buddhist scholars for centuries, it requires a two-to-three-hour hike from the nearest village — no road reaches it. In winter, heavy snow cuts the monastery off entirely, with supplies carried in by mules.

Planning and Permits

The travel window for all seven destinations runs roughly June to September, when roads are open and high passes accessible. Border-adjacent areas — Turtuk, Hanle, and Dha-Hanu — require an Inner Line Permit for Indian nationals and a Protected Area Permit for foreign travellers, both arranged easily in Leh. Carry multiple physical copies; checkpoints along these routes often lack internet connectivity for digital verification.

Mobile coverage is patchy to non-existent across most of these destinations. ATMs are rare outside Leh. Homestays are the backbone of accommodation — often the only option, and almost always the most rewarding one.

Why Offbeat Ladakh Matters Now

The 43% tourism surge is good news for Ladakh's economy, but it has also sharpened concerns about environmental pressure on fragile ecosystems. Policymakers have begun promoting electric vehicles, reducing plastic waste, and encouraging community-based eco-tourism, according to The Hindu Business Line. Spreading visitor traffic beyond Pangong and Nubra into these seven destinations is not just a richer travel experience — it is part of the sustainability equation Ladakh urgently needs.
